chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Samaan, who said:

I asked him about the skin of the female animal that has died (maitah) which has been salted, and it is the kaimukht (tanned leather), so he granted permission regarding it, and said: 'And if you do not touch it, it is better.'

The resolution between these two narrations is that we should attribute them to a form of taqiyya (dissimulation/prudence), because the skin of the maitah does not become pure through tanning (dabagh) in our view, as we have clarified in the Book of Salat.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةُ: Taqiyya (prudent dissimulation or concealment of a ruling due to fear or context)
key_terms.الدَّبَاغُ: Tawing (the process of treating animal skin to make it usable and pure)
key_terms.جِلْدُ الْمَيْتَةِ: Skin of the animal that died a natural death (not slaughtered ritually)

ai.seo_question: Does tawing purify the skin of an animal that died a natural death (maitah) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Istibsar clarifies the status of salted animal hides (kaimukht) that died a natural death (maitah), where the Imam permits use but prefers avoidance. The apparent contradiction with the general Shia ruling that tawing does not purify maitah skin is resolved by attributing the permission to taqiyya (dissimulation), reflecting the historical context of political pressure on the Imams. This highlights the nuanced application of ritual purity laws in Shia jurisprudence, balancing textual literalism with practical religious reality.
